notes.b: Overpopulation is about the balance between people and what they have to live on, not about how crowded a place looks. Two places with the same number of people can be very differently placed.
points: Overpopulation: the population of an area is too large for its resources, technology and economy to support an acceptable standard of living.
It is a balance between people and resources, not a matter of numbers or density (people per square kilometre) alone.
Underpopulation: too few people to develop the resources fully, so some resources go unused.
Optimum population: the number that gives the highest standard of living with existing resources and technology.
The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² (2020s) and is densely populated but not overpopulated, because its wealth, technology and trade let it support them well.
The Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) is thinly populated but overpopulated, because its fragile resources, drought and poverty cannot support its people.
Niger, a Sahel country, has about 27 million people (2023) in a very large, mostly desert country, so little of the land can feed anyone.
notes.tip: Never say overpopulation means high density. Examiners reward the distinction, so use the Netherlands (dense, not overpopulated) against the Sahel (thin, overpopulated). Questions ask what overpopulation means, so define it as a balance of people, resources, technology and economy.

notes.b: Thinkers have long argued about whether population or resources win out. Three views are worth knowing, each with a date and a title.
points: Malthus, 'An Essay on the Principle of Population' (1798): population grows geometrically (doubling again and again) while food grows arithmetically (by a fixed amount each time), so famine, disease and war act as positive checks that cut numbers back.
Ireland's Great Famine is often cited in support of Malthus.
Boserup, 'The Conditions of Agricultural Growth' (1965): population pressure drives farming innovation, so food supply can rise to meet demand.
The Green Revolution (the spread of high-yield crops and modern farming from the mid-1960s) is often cited in support of Boserup.
Club of Rome, 'The Limits to Growth' (1972): argues that growth is limited by finite resources.
notes.tip: Malthus wrote in 1798, not 1898, and Boserup in 1965. Do not attribute 'The Limits to Growth' to Malthus: it is the Club of Rome.

notes.b: Resources are what a population lives on. Where they are not developed, are degraded or shrink, the same population becomes too many.
points: Sahel: desertification (fertile land turning to desert), drought, overgrazing, fuelwood cutting and the shrinking of Lake Chad all cut what the land can support.
Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s, because of irrigation demand and drought, which is a resource shrinking under the same population.
Pre-Famine Ireland: over-reliance on one resource, the potato, and subdivision of holdings (farms split among sons) into ever-smaller plots, so many families had too little land.
Developing resources raises carrying capacity (the number of people an area can support): India's Green Revolution and Ireland's industrial growth since the 1960s.
notes.tip: Each factor in an essay needs at least two named case studies, so pair the Sahel and pre-Famine Ireland, then contrast with India or Ireland where developed resources raised carrying capacity.

notes.h: Pre-Famine Ireland: dependence on the potato
notes.b: Ireland shows how one fragile resource can leave a large population exposed. Here the checked facts are the whole-island figures and the blight.
points: The population of the whole island was about 8.2 million in 1841; use this whole-island figure, not the 26-county one.
The rural poor depended heavily on the potato, so they had no other food when it failed.
Holdings were subdivided among sons into ever-smaller plots, and landlords were often absentee (living elsewhere).
Conacre meant renting a small plot for one season.
Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans, a disease of potato plants) struck in 1845, and the Great Famine ran from 1845 to 1849.
About 1 million people died and about 1 million emigrated, leaving a whole-island population of about 6.6 million by 1851.
notes.tip: The Great Famine began in 1845. The 8.2 million figure is the whole island, so do not mix it with the 26-county figure of about 6.5 million.

notes.b: Desertification (fertile land turning to desert) is the clearest case of resources shrinking under pressure. It happens because a poor, fast-growing population overuses a dry land.
points: The Sahel is a semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan.
Rainfall is about 200–600 mm a year, falls in a short summer rainy season and is very unreliable, so crops and grass can fail.

Causes of desertification: overgrazing (too many animals for the grass), overcultivation with fallow periods (rests that let soil recover) abandoned, cutting trees and shrubs for fuelwood, and drought.
Wind and rain then erode the bare soil, because nothing is left to hold it in place.

notes.b: People and governments have tried to reverse desertification by holding water and soil in place and by bringing back trees.
points: The Great Green Wall, an African Union initiative launched in 2007, aims to restore a belt of land across the Sahel.
Stone lines (diguettes) along contours (lines of equal height) and zaï planting pits in Burkina Faso trap water and soil, so crops can grow on degraded ground.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees in Niger lets farmers protect and regrow trees that spring from existing roots and stumps.

notes.b: Attitudes and customs affect how many children people have, and so how fast a population grows against its resources.
points: Factors include religion and attitudes to contraception (methods of avoiding pregnancy), the status and education of women, early marriage, preference for sons, children as farm labour and old-age security, and the prestige of large families.
notes.tip: A question on this factor needs at least two named case studies. Use Niger and the Sahel, India (Kerala against Bihar) and Ireland before and after the 1970s.

notes.h: Society and culture: Niger and the Sahel
notes.b: Niger shows what happens when several of these cultural factors act together.
points: Early marriage of girls is common, so women start having children young and have more of them over their lives.
Female literacy is low, which limits women's choices and their use of family planning.
Large families carry prestige, so having many children raises a family's standing.
Total fertility rate (the average number of children a woman has in her lifetime) is about 6 (early 2020s), among the highest in the world, with population growth over 3% a year.

Median age (the age that splits the population in half) is about 15, so the population is very young, and Niger is among the lowest-ranked countries in the UN Human Development Index (a ranking of countries by health, education and income) (2020s).
notes.tip: Use only the Niger figures given here. Do not give percentages for female literacy or growth rates from model answers, as many of those are invented.

notes.h: Society and culture: India, Kerala and Bihar
notes.b: Within India, two states show how education and the status of women change family size.
points: Son preference and the low status of women in some Indian states keep families having children until they have sons.
Kerala: total fertility rate about 1.8 (National Family Health Survey 2019–21), literacy about 94% (Census 2011), the highest of any state, with high female literacy and good health care.
Bihar: total fertility rate about 3.0 (National Family Health Survey 2019–21), literacy about 62% (Census 2011), the lowest of any state.
India's total fertility rate is about 2.0 (2019–21), down from about 6 in the 1950s.

notes.h: Society and culture: Ireland before and after the 1970s
notes.b: Ireland shows culture changing fertility within living memory, as law and attitudes shifted.
points: Before the 1970s, Catholic teaching, large families and illegal contraception kept fertility high.
Births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980.
Contraception was legalised by the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, on prescription, so couples could plan family size legally.

The total fertility rate (average children per woman) was about 4 in the early 1970s, fell below replacement (the level at which each generation just replaces itself) around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level questions on how culture and society have affected Ireland's population, use the fertility fall from about 4 to about 1.5 and the change in attitudes and law.

notes.b: Income and family size are linked in both directions. Poor families tend to have more children, and large families make it harder to escape poverty.
points: Low-income countries have high birth rates: children are economic assets (they work and earn), infant mortality is high so parents have extra children, and there are no pensions, so children support parents in old age.
Rising incomes bring falling fertility, through the cost of raising children, women's paid work and education.
Poverty also limits the ability to develop resources or import food, so a poor country cannot easily make up for a shortage.
Contrast low-income Niger with high-income Ireland, the EU and Japan.
notes.tip: Contrast low-income Niger with high-income Ireland, the EU and Japan. Use Bangladesh only for its fertility fall, never as overpopulated because it is dense.

notes.h: High-income contrasts: Ireland, the EU and Japan
notes.b: High-income countries show where rising incomes lead: low fertility, long lives and, in Japan, an ageing and shrinking population.
points: Ireland: total fertility rate about 1.5 (2023); life expectancy (average years a person lives) about 82–83 years.
EU: total fertility rate about 1.4 (2023).
Japan: about 29% aged 65 or over (2023); population falling from a peak of about 128 million around 2008–2010.
Bangladesh is an exception: its fertility fell sharply while it was still poor.

notes.b: Bangladesh shows that fertility can fall without wealth when policy, education and women's work change.
points: Independent since 1971, so its fertility fall happened within a few decades of nationhood.
Total fertility rate fell, for example, from about 6–7 in the early 1970s to about 2 in the 2020s.

Reasons: a national family planning programme with community health workers visiting homes, NGOs (non-governmental organisations, such as charities), girls' education and millions of women employed in the garment industry.
Population density is over 1,100 people per km² (2020s), one of the highest of any large country; it is used here for its fertility fall, not as overpopulation.
notes.tip: Bangladesh is very dense, but it is used here for its fertility fall. Do not call it overpopulated because it is dense.

notes.b: Technology changes both sides of the balance. It lowers deaths, raises food output and lowers births, and where it is missing, it keeps carrying capacity low.
points: Medical technology (vaccines, antibiotics, clean water) cut death rates far faster than birth rates fell, causing the population explosion of the 20th century; this is DTM (demographic transition model) stage 2 in Changing population characteristics.
Penicillin (an antibiotic) was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980.
Agricultural technology: the Green Revolution, with high-yield seeds, irrigation and fertilisers, increased carrying capacity.
Contraceptive technology lowered birth rates, because couples could choose family size.
Lack of technology: subsistence farming (growing food mainly for the family's own use) keeps carrying capacity low in the Sahel.
notes.tip: A technology answer should show both sides: medical technology raised population, while agricultural technology raised carrying capacity and contraceptive technology lowered births.

notes.b: India shows technology raising carrying capacity, but with costs that you must also give.
points: Green Revolution from the mid-1960s: high-yield wheat bred in Mexico by Norman Borlaug, introduced in India under M. S. Swaminathan.
Food-grain output rose, for example, from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million tonnes (2022–23).
Core areas: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
Side effects: falling water tables (the underground water level, which drops when too much is pumped for irrigation), soil degradation and debt among small farmers.
notes.tip: Do not call India's Green Revolution an unqualified success. Give its side effects as well as the rise in output.

notes.b: Governments can try to change birth rates directly. Policies that aim to cut births are called anti-natalist, and they can succeed but carry a human cost.
points: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952.
Forced sterilisations (operations that end a person's ability to have children) during the Emergency, 1975–77, caused a backlash against family planning.
China's one-child policy was introduced in 1979–80.

notes.b: China's policy cut fertility sharply, but its enforcement and its effects on the population show the human cost.
points: Enforced through fines, loss of jobs and benefits, and in places forced abortions and sterilisations.
Exceptions existed for many rural families whose first child was a girl and for ethnic minorities, so it did not apply to every family.

Effects: fertility fell well below replacement; the sex ratio at birth (boys born per 100 girls) rose above 115 in the 2000s, through son preference and sex-selective abortion, leaving millions more men than women.
The '4-2-1' problem: four grandparents, two parents and one child per family, so one child may support six older people.
Rapid ageing followed, because fewer young people replaced older ones.
Replaced by a two-child policy from 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021.
China's population fell in 2022, the first fall since 1961.
notes.tip: Say that the policy had exceptions and do not state it applied to every family. Do not give the Chinese government's claim of 400 million births prevented as fact.

notes.h: Effects of overpopulation: food and environment
notes.b: When there are too many people for the land, the first effects are on food and on the land itself.
points: Food shortages, malnutrition (not enough food or the wrong nutrients) and famine.
Environmental damage: soil erosion, desertification, deforestation, overgrazing and water shortages, because people strip the land to get food and fuel.
The Sahel shows both: famines in the late 1960s–1970s and the early-to-mid 1980s, and desertification.
notes.tip: Questions ask for causes and effects of overpopulation with examples, so tie each effect to a place such as the Sahel.

notes.h: Effects of overpopulation: economy and services
notes.b: Too many people for the jobs and services available means poverty and strain on public provision.
points: Unemployment (no work) and underemployment (part-time or low-productivity work, below what a person could do), poverty and low incomes.
Pressure on schools, hospitals, housing, water and sanitation, because these cannot expand as fast as the population.
A high young dependency ratio: many children per worker, so each worker supports more people who do not earn.

notes.h: Effects of overpopulation: migration and conflict
notes.b: When an area cannot support its people, some leave and others compete for what remains.
points: Rural-to-urban migration to shanty towns (areas of poor, self-built housing on the edge of cities). There is more on this in Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions.
Emigration, as people leave the country in search of work or food.
Conflict over land and water, because shrinking resources are fought over.

notes.h: Growth rates and development: rapid growth
notes.b: The speed of population growth affects how fast a country can develop. Rapid growth tends to hold development back.
points: Savings go on feeding and educating more people rather than investment, so there is less money for factories and infrastructure.
Per-capita income (income per person) gains are cancelled out, because the extra output is shared among more people.
Jobs cannot keep up with population growth, and the environment is degraded.
The 'poverty trap' of high fertility keeps families and countries poor.

notes.h: Growth rates and development: slowing growth
notes.b: When growth slows, development can speed up. Fewer children means a bigger share of the population is of working age.
points: The demographic dividend is a large working-age population with fewer dependants (children and older people who rely on others).
East Asian economies such as South Korea and China, and Ireland from the 1990s, benefited.
Ireland's dividend: the large generation born around 1980 (births peaked at about 74,000 that year) entered the workforce in the late 1990s and 2000s, helping the Celtic Tiger economy.
notes.tip: Use the demographic dividend as your example of slowing growth helping development. Name South Korea, China and Ireland from the 1990s.

notes.h: Growth rates and development: very slow or negative growth
notes.b: Very slow growth or falling population also harms development, because the population ages.
points: Ageing, labour shortages, a shrinking tax base (fewer workers paying tax) and high pension and health costs.
Examples: Japan, Italy and South Korea, all countries with very low fertility.
Italy: total fertility rate about 1.2 (2023).
South Korea: total fertility rate about 0.7 (2023), the lowest in the world.

keyTerms.definition: The condition in which an area's population is too large for its resources, technology and economy to support an acceptable standard of living.
A population too small to develop an area's resources fully.
The population that gives the highest standard of living with existing resources and technology.
The population an area can support at an acceptable standard of living with its resources and technology.
Factors such as famine, disease and war that halt population growth when it outstrips food supply, in Malthus's theory.
The spread of desert-like conditions as overgrazing, overcultivation, fuelwood cutting and drought degrade the soil.
The introduction of high-yield seeds, irrigation and fertilisers that raised food production from the mid-1960s.
The economic gain from a large working-age population with fewer dependants.
The cycle in which high fertility keeps families and countries poor, and poverty keeps fertility high.
China's policy from 1979–80 limiting most families to one child, enforced through fines, loss of benefits and in places forced abortion and sterilisation.

factCards.term: Density is not overpopulation: two contrasting examples
factCards.definition: The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² but is not overpopulated, thanks to wealth, technology and trade. The Sahel is thinly populated but overpopulated, because its fragile resources, drought and poverty cannot support its people.

factCards.term: Population theories: Malthus, Boserup and the Club of Rome
factCards.definition: Malthus (1798): population grows geometrically and food arithmetically, so famine, disease and war check growth. Boserup (1965): population pressure drives farming innovation, so food supply can rise. Club of Rome, The Limits to Growth (1972).

Overgrazing, overcultivation as fallow periods are abandoned, and cutting trees and shrubs for fuelwood strip the land; drought dries it out; wind and rain then erode the bare soil. Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s.

The Great Green Wall, an African Union initiative launched in 2007, to restore a belt of land across the Sahel; stone lines (diguettes) along contours and zaï planting pits in Burkina Faso to trap water and soil; farmer-managed regeneration of trees in Niger.

factCards.term: Niger: how society and culture keep growth high
factCards.definition: Early marriage of girls is common, female literacy is low and large families carry prestige. Fertility is about 6 children per woman, growth over 3% a year and median age about 15; Niger is among the lowest-ranked in the UN Human Development Index.

factCards.term: Pre-Famine Ireland: why it was overpopulated
factCards.definition: About 8.2 million people on the whole island in 1841; the rural poor depended heavily on one resource, the potato; holdings were subdivided among sons into ever-smaller plots; landlords were often absent; conacre rented small plots for one season.

Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) struck in 1845; about 1 million people died and about 1 million emigrated, and the island's population fell to about 6.6 million by 1851. It is often cited in support of Malthus.

factCards.term: Effects of overpopulation: six to name
factCards.definition: Food shortages and famine (Sahel: late 1960s–1970s, early-to-mid 1980s); soil erosion, desertification and water shortages; unemployment and poverty; pressure on schools, hospitals and housing; migration to cities and abroad; conflict over land and water.

Kerala: fertility about 1.8 (2019–21), literacy about 94% (2011), the highest of any state, with high female literacy and good health care. Bihar: fertility about 3.0 and literacy about 62%, the lowest. India as a whole: 943 females per 1,000 males (2011).

factCards.term: Income levels: why poor countries have high birth rates
factCards.definition: In low-income countries children are economic assets, infant mortality is high and there are no pensions. As incomes rise, children cost more and women work and study, so fertility falls: Niger about 6, Ireland about 1.5, the EU about 1.4 (2023).

factCards.term: Bangladesh: how fertility fell while the country was still poor
factCards.definition: Fertility fell from about 6–7 in the early 1970s to about 2 in the 2020s through a national family planning programme with community health workers visiting homes, NGOs, girls' education, and millions of women employed in the garment industry.

factCards.term: Technology and population growth: four impacts
factCards.definition: Medical technology (vaccines, antibiotics, clean water; penicillin 1928; smallpox eradicated 1980) cut death rates faster than birth rates; the Green Revolution raised carrying capacity; contraception cut birth rates; subsistence farming limits the Sahel.

factCards.term: India's Green Revolution: what it achieved and its side effects
factCards.definition: From the mid-1960s, high-yield seeds (wheat bred by Norman Borlaug, introduced under M. S. Swaminathan), irrigation and fertilisers raised yields; food-grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million (2022–23). Side effects: lower water tables, soil damage, debt.

factCards.term: India's family planning: two key events
factCards.definition: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952. Forced sterilisations during the Emergency (1975–77) caused a backlash. Fertility has fallen from about 6 in the 1950s to about 2.0 (2019–21).

factCards.term: China's one-child policy: exceptions and later changes
factCards.definition: Introduced in 1979–80, with exceptions for many rural families whose first child was a girl and for ethnic minorities. Replaced by a two-child policy from 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021; China's population fell in 2022, the first fall since 1961.

Fertility fell well below replacement; son preference and sex-selective abortion pushed the sex ratio at birth above 115 boys per 100 girls in the 2000s, leaving millions more men; the 4-2-1 family (four grandparents, two parents, one child); rapid ageing.

factCards.term: How rapid population growth slows development
factCards.definition: Savings go on feeding and educating more people instead of investment; per-capita income gains are cancelled out; jobs cannot keep up; the environment is degraded; high fertility traps families and countries in poverty.

East Asian economies such as South Korea and China; Ireland from the 1990s, when the large generation born around 1980 (births peaked at about 74,000) entered the workforce in the late 1990s and 2000s, helping the Celtic Tiger.

factCards.term: Very slow or negative growth: effects on development
factCards.definition: Ageing, labour shortages, a shrinking tax base and high pension and health costs, as in Japan, Italy (fertility about 1.2, 2023) and South Korea (fertility about 0.7, 2023, the lowest in the world).

questions.prompt: Examine the causes and effects of overpopulation, with reference to an example you have studied.
questions.model: Overpopulation exists when an area's population is too large for its resources, technology and economy to support an acceptable standard of living. The Sahel, with Niger as its example, shows the causes. Fertility is high: the total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman, and population growth is over 3% a year. Culture sustains this, through early marriage of girls, low female literacy and the prestige of large families. Resources are degraded: overgrazing, overcultivation, cutting trees for fuelwood and drought cause desertification, and Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s. Technology is low: subsistence farming keeps carrying capacity low. The effects are food shortages and famine, as in the droughts and famines of the late 1960s–1970s and the early-to-mid 1980s, environmental damage through soil erosion and desertification, poverty, unemployment and pressure on services, and migration and conflict over land and water. Responses include the Great Green Wall, launched in 2007, stone lines and zaï pits in Burkina Faso, and farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees in Niger.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of society and culture on levels of population growth, with reference to example(s) you have studied.
questions.model: In the Sahel and Niger, culture keeps fertility high. Early marriage of girls is common, female literacy is low, and large families carry prestige, so the total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman and growth is over 3% a year. India shows the contrast between states. Son preference and the low status of women in some states keep fertility high, while Kerala, with literacy about 94% (Census 2011), high female literacy and good health care, has a total fertility rate of about 1.8, against about 3.0 in Bihar, where literacy is about 62%. China's one-child policy, from 1979–80, used fines, loss of jobs and benefits and in places forced abortion, while exceptions existed for many rural families whose first child was a girl. Son preference and sex-selective abortion pushed the sex ratio at birth above 115 boys per 100 girls in the 2000s. Ireland before the 1970s had Catholic teaching, large families and illegal contraception; births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980, and contraception was legalised in 1979, after which fertility fell below replacement around 1990.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of technology on levels of population growth.
questions.model: Medical technology, such as vaccines, antibiotics and clean water, cut death rates far faster than birth rates fell, causing the population explosion of the 20th century and rapid growth in developing countries. Contraceptive technology lowered birth rates where it was available: Bangladesh's total fertility rate fell from about 6–7 in the early 1970s to about 2 in the 2020s, helped by a family planning programme with community health workers. Agricultural technology raised carrying capacity: the Green Revolution, from the mid-1960s, bred high-yield wheat and introduced irrigation and fertilisers, and India's food-grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million tonnes (2022–23). Its side effects include falling water tables, soil degradation and debt among small farmers, so it did not fully resolve pressure on resources. In the Sahel, lack of technology keeps subsistence farming low-yielding and carrying capacity low. Pre-Famine Ireland shows the same limit: dependence on the potato, a single low-technology resource, left the population exposed when blight struck in 1845.
